answer.headline: FAA large_hub NAS delay is uneven, and the peak-hour association has no established sign
answer.body:
Over {F31.period}, calculated NAS delay minutes per arrival across FAA large_hub airports (hub class L) is {F31} at {F31.label}, {F32} at {F32.label}, {F33} at {F33.label}, {F34} at {F34.label}, and {F35} at {F35.label}. These percentiles are {F31.class}.

Ordered from the highest calculated NAS delay, SFO is {F63} with relative rank score {F66}, LGA is {F54} with relative rank score {F67}, EWR is {F46} with relative rank score {F68}, ORD is {F58} with relative rank score {F69}, and BOS is {F39} with relative rank score {F70}. SLC is the low end of the same ranking at {F64}. The relative scores {F66}, {F67}, {F68}, {F69}, and {F70} are not equal, so that ordering has no tie. No large_hub airport was left unscored. This is a delay ranking inside the set, not an investment screen and not a valuation, so it has no screening flags.

Observed scheduled peak-hour operations at those high-delay airports are {F153} at SFO, {F144} at LGA, {F136} at EWR, {F148} at ORD, and {F129} at BOS. A correlation using only that high-delay slice cannot be estimated: the operator returned insufficient_data. Across the full large_hub set, the calculated Pearson correlation of NAS delay with scheduled peak-hour operations is {F156} and the calculated Spearman rank correlation is {F157}. The Spearman bootstrap interval runs from {F158} to {F159} and uses {F160}. The interval contains negative and positive values, so the sign of the rank association is not established. That association is calculated across airports. It is not a cause, not a forecast, and not evidence of unmet demand, terminal capacity, fares, or profitability.

Calculated On-Time coverage over {F181.period} is {F181} at EWR, {F198} at SFO, {F189} at LGA, {F193} at ORD, and {F174} at BOS. The partial-slice caveat applies to EWR {F181}, IAD {F184}, IAH {F185}, JFK {F186}, and MIA {F191}. The delay and peak-hour window is {F31.period}.

claims.text: Over {F31.period}, the calculated distribution of NAS delay minutes per arrival across the FAA large_hub set is {F31} ({F31.label}), {F32} ({F32.label}), {F33} ({F33.label}), {F34} ({F34.label}), and {F35} ({F35.label}).

SFO calculated NAS delay is {F63} and its relative rank score is {F66}. LGA calculated NAS delay is {F54} and its relative rank score is {F67}. EWR calculated NAS delay is {F46} and its relative rank score is {F68}. ORD calculated NAS delay is {F58} and its relative rank score is {F69}. BOS calculated NAS delay is {F39} and its relative rank score is {F70}. SLC calculated NAS delay, the low end of the same ranking, is {F64}.

The relative scores for SFO, LGA, EWR, ORD, and BOS are not equal, so the high-delay ordering has no tie. The ranking is a within-set delay order, not an investment screen, and it produces no screening flags.
Observed scheduled peak-hour operations are {F153} at SFO, {F144} at LGA, {F136} at EWR, {F148} at ORD, and {F129} at BOS.

Across the full large_hub set, the calculated Pearson correlation of NAS delay with scheduled peak-hour operations is {F156}, the calculated Spearman rank correlation is {F157}, the Spearman bootstrap interval runs from {F158} to {F159}, and the airports used are {F160}.

The Spearman interval contains both negative and positive values, so the sign of the rank association between NAS delay and scheduled peak-hour operations is not established. The result is an association across airports, not a cause.
Calculated On-Time coverage over {F181.period} is {F181} at EWR, {F198} at SFO, {F189} at LGA, {F193} at ORD, and {F174} at BOS.
The partial-slice coverage caveat is attached to EWR {F181}, IAD {F184}, IAH {F185}, JFK {F186}, and MIA {F191}.
EWR calculated NAS delay {F46} and observed peak-hour operations {F136} describe a partial On-Time slice, because EWR coverage {F181} carries the partial-slice caveat.

assumptions: Large hubs are FAA hub class L, the large_hub set. resolve_entities returned unknown for the phrases large hubs, large hub, and large_hub, so the analysis uses the hub_class group filter.
Worst means the highest calculated NAS delay minutes per arrival. The rank gives a higher delay a higher relative score, scaled within this set. Scores change if airports are added or removed.
Peak hour ops means the catalog scheduled peak-hour metric (the percentile measure), not the single busiest scheduled hour.
The reported correlation uses the full large_hub set over the same T12 window as the distribution. A correlation limited to the high-delay airports alone is not what was estimated.
The window is the default T12, which resolved to {F31.period} for NAS delay and for scheduled peak-hour operations.
limitations: On-Time covers domestic flights of reporting carriers only, with no international flights and no small carriers. NAS delay is calculated airspace and system delay minutes per operated arrival. The cause of those minutes is not identified.
Scheduled peak-hour operations are a lower bound on total scheduled operations because they count reporting carriers only.
On-Time coverage is measured on {F181.period}, which is not the same window label as the delay and peak-hour figures {F31.period}, because coverage uses months shared with T-100.
EWR is in the high-delay group and carries the partial-slice coverage caveat, as do IAD, IAH, JFK, and MIA. Those airports remain inside the distribution and the full-set correlation.
A correlation using only the high-delay airports cannot be estimated: the operator returned insufficient_data because that slice is smaller than the minimum sample a correlation requires.
The correlation does not control for size, hub role, or region. It is not evidence of unmet demand, terminal capacity, fares, or profitability, none of which these metrics measure.
Rank scores are relative to this large_hub set. They are not a valuation and they are not the investment screening model, so screening flags are not part of the result.
